entities.name: Cai Yong
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Cai Yong (133–192 CE), a polymath of the Eastern Han dynasty, stands as a pivotal figure in Chinese intellectual history, celebrated for his profound scholarship, calligraphy, music, and official service. His life, spanning the turbulent decades leading to the Han collapse, uniquely intertwines with the preservation of classical texts and the development of scholarly traditions. Operating primarily within the imperial capital of Luoyang and later Chang'an, Cai Yong's influence reached across the literate elite, shaping standards for textual accuracy and artistic expression during a period of immense political and social upheaval. He is particularly renowned for his role in standardizing the Five Classics through stone inscription, an endeavor aimed at preserving Confucian orthodoxy against corruption and factionalism.

Born in Qi County, Chenliu Commandery (modern-day Qi County, Kaifeng, Henan), Cai Yong rose through the ranks of officialdom, serving under Emperors Ling and Xian. His most monumental achievement was supervising the inscription of the Xiping Stone Classics onto steles outside the imperial academy in Luoyang between 175 and 183 CE. This project, which meticulously carved the standardized texts of the *Book of Changes*, *Book of Documents*, *Book of Odes*, *Rites of Zhou*, *Yi Li*, *Gongyang Commentary*, and *Analects* in three scripts (ancient, seal, and clerical), provided an authoritative, unalterable version for scholars to copy and reference, profoundly impacting textual transmission for centuries. Beyond this, Cai Yong was a master calligrapher, famed for his *bafen* (clerical script), and a gifted musician who composed and reformed ceremonial music. His literary output included numerous essays, poems, and historical works, though many are now lost.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Cai Yong's work on the Xiping Stone Classics set a precedent for state-sponsored textual standardization, influencing the transmission of Confucianism for over a millennium. His artistic contributions in calligraphy also profoundly shaped Chinese aesthetic traditions.
